terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; most often in the participle perculsus
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.3.132 (Lewis & Short): haec tē vōx nōn perculit? nōn perturbāvit?
terms.comment: Literally to knock over, a cart or a tree; of the mind, to strike with dismay, to stun (Lewis & Short). Traupman’s “downhearted” is animō perculsō esse (p. 151).

terms.gloss: strike; shock, make a strong impression on
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.25.3: repente percussus est atrōcissimīs litterīs
terms.comment: To strike or pierce; of news or words, to shock, and also simply to strike someone as odd (percussit animum, “it struck me”, Cic. Att. 4.8b.3, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.4.1: valdē priōre pāginā perturbātus
terms.comment: Upset and confused rather than stunned (see don’t be upset, affect).

evidence: Liv. 28.25.5 (Lewis & Short): quae causa īrae cōnsternātiōnisque subitae foret
terms.comment: Not before Augustus, and mostly in the historians (Lewis & Short). For “it was a shock” in everyday speech, a verb is more natural: graviter commōtus sum.

phrases.latin: is cum ad mē Laudicēam vēnisset mēcumque ego eum esse vellem, repente percussus est atrōcissimīs litterīs
phrases.english: he had come to me at Laodicea, and I wanted him with me, when suddenly he was shocked by the most dreadful letter

phrases.latin: sed hoc scītō, tuōs veterēs hostīs, novōs amīcōs, vehementer litterīs perculsōs
phrases.english: but know this: your old enemies, your new friends, were badly shaken by the letter

phrases.latin: haec tē vōx nōn perculit? nōn perturbāvit?
phrases.english: didn’t these words shock you? didn’t they upset you?
